You are an independent reviewer of an economic microsimulation (the Compassionism Simulation). Read the material below and answer under these headings:
1. Is the diagnosis right? Does the evidence show that the private businesses' lagged price, and not something else, causes the two-year swing?
2. Is calling it a defect (not a reading of the design) justified by the design text quoted?
3. Is the fix correct? Check the algebra of the at-sale price (vK, the per-adult cut with a budget limit, the advance and its repayment, the share of BU attributed to private businesses), and the code diff. Name any case where it double-counts, loses money, or departs from the design.
4. Is anything the fix changes not covered by the preregistration's outcomes or checks?
5. Are the preregistration's decision rules sound and fixed before the run? Anything that could let a result be chosen after seeing it?
6. Is the plain-words report accurate and fair to the evidence (no overclaiming)?
7. The three most important changes you would make.
Be concrete; quote the text you refer to.

=== The plain-words report ===
# The BU's two-year swing: a private business's lower BU price paid a year late

Nov 18, 2026. Written by Claude. A plain-words report of research-update step S90; the full decision is in `dev/DECISIONS.md` ("S90").

## What was seen

In the main row (full backing, flat prices; Reference environment, seed 1, 500 adults), the Basic Units (BU) each adult spends on the cost of living swing from year to year: $22,838 in years 0 and 1, then $10,969, $21,452, $13,819, $19,472, $16,202, and so on. The swing shrinks each year but takes more than ten years to die out. Meanwhile the BU paid each month keep their value and the cost of living hardly moves. The swing is in every programme row, and it was behind the swing in the cash share that the supply study (S82) found.

## What causes it

The BU an adult receives in a year (about $24,900) are less than the essentials bill (about $30,000), so every BU is spent unless a price cut lowers the bill first. Two price cuts do that, and both are paid from the businesses' conversion premium (an essential-service business converts the BU it accepts into dollars at three times face value; the extra is the premium):

1. the cut that community-owned businesses (PTFs) give from their share of the premium;
2. the lower BU price that privately owned businesses give from theirs.

A trace of one run, turning each cut off in a copy of the engine (never the engine itself), shows that the private businesses' price causes the swing. With the community cut off, the swing stays; with the private price off, it goes.

The private price was paid from **last year's** premium. A large cut this year means fewer BU spent this year, so less premium, so a smaller cut next year, and so on: the BU spent alternate above and below the level where the cut equals the premium it earns. Average incomes swing with them ($72,358, $92,808, $81,544, $98,970 in years 1-4), because the conversion and the workers' share of the premium follow the BU spent.

## Design or defect

A defect. Duke's design (Oct 1) sets the private price at the sale:

> A privately owned ESP cuts its prices for customers paying in BU so that it stays revenue neutral. At a 3x conversion rate, a $9 / $12 / $15 menu becomes $3 / $4 / $5 in BU.

The model's own decision for that step said the same ("one BU buys as many essentials as the conversion rate in dollars"), but the code paid the premium a year late. The lag is not in the design, and it is what makes the swing.

## The fix (built, off until a rerun)

A new option of the surplus split, `vAt: 'sale'`, sets the private price at the sale. One BU spent at a private business buys 1 + vK dollars of essentials, where vK is the premium the business will earn on that BU (after the conversion tax and the share kept for business payroll) less the workers' share of it. In the main row vK is about 0.90 at first and 0.81 once community capacity is reached (0.79 and 0.71 in the Stress Test): a BU spent there buys about $1.90 of essentials rather than Duke's $3, because the conversion tax, payroll and the workers' match come out of the premium too. That is the same price, on average, as the lagged rule settled to; only its timing changes. The cut is paid as an advance, and next year's premium repays it exactly. One small part cannot be known at the sale: payroll BU that a business could not pay out and converts the next year. That part is shared a year late, as before ($305 per adult in year 1, $73 in year 2, $4 in year 3, then nothing in the main row).

With the option on, the swing is gone in all three environments: the BU spent per adult in Reference run $16,815, $16,590, $17,392, $17,592, $17,981, and stay within $16,236-18,195 after that, and incomes rise smoothly.

The option is off by default, so every published figure is unchanged and the registered v5.9 model can still be reproduced (the guard test is identical in every output).

## What it reaches

Every programme row uses the private rule, so every published programme figure since v5.0 (Oct 2, 2026) is reached. This includes the v5.9 main rows and readings, the central-bank and history studies, and the supply study. A first look on two seeds (not a result) shows small changes, all in the programme's favour: the cut in basket poverty grows by about 0.6-0.7 points (Reference: 32.3 to 33.0 points), the deepest-poverty measure (FGT2) by about 0.1, and median real wealth by $200-1,200. The preregistered rerun (research-update `prereg/2026-11-s90-private-price-at-sale.md`) will measure the change on 500 paired seeds in all three environments. Its results will be published whichever way they come out. Until then the swing is a stated limit of every programme row.

## What the community businesses' cut does

The community businesses' cut stays as it is: their premium is split three ways (price cuts, reinvestment, workers) once the year's surplus is known, which is a reading of their design. With the private price at the sale, it shows no swing.

=== The decision record ===
## S90 (Nov 18, 2026): the two-year cycle in the BU's relief traced to a one-year lag in the private ESPs' lower BU price; an at-sale price built behind a switch (`sp.vAt`)
- **Question.** In the main row (full backing, flat prices; Reference, seed 1, 500 adults) the BU spent per adult runs $22,838 (years 0-1), then $10,969, $21,452, $13,819, $19,472, $16,202: a damped two-year cycle, while the BU paid per month holds its real value. Which term moves, and is it the design or a defect?
- **How it was traced.** `dev/tools/s90_trace.js` runs its own copy of the built engine with read-only probes (as `s66_trace.js` does; `--check` proves the copy gives the harness's outputs exactly, 991 keys) and prints, per year, the BU issued, the essentials bill, the price cuts, the BU spent and expired, the relief `tbAccount` books, and the surplus split's pool. The relief booked (`a._slBU`) is the BU spent (`fwB`) less the grocery cut; the BU budget (about $24,900) is below the essentials bill (about $30,000), so the BU spent move one for one with the price cuts paid before them. Two cuts are paid that way, both funded from last year's conversion premium: the PTFs' uniform price cut (d98) and the private ESPs' lower BU price (plan step 14, d140). Turned off one at a time in the tool's copy (never the engine): with the PTF cut off the cycle stays (BU spent $12,621, $20,987, $16,434, $19,677); with the private price off it goes (BU spent $23,394, $23,647, $23,287, $22,934, smooth); with both off the BU spent are flat. The same in Adverse and Stress.
- **The mechanism.** The private price is paid from last year's private premium, which is earned on last year's BU spent at private ESPs. A large cut this year means fewer BU spent this year, so a smaller premium and a smaller cut next year: a feedback with a one-year lag, so the BU spent alternate around the level where the cut equals the premium it earns. The cut is about 0.7-0.85 times last year's BU spent, so the swing shrinks by that factor a year. It reaches incomes (mean income per adult in the main row: $72,358, $92,808, $81,544, $98,970, $91,093) through the conversion and the workers' match, and every figure built on BU spent, expired BU, project hiring or programme cost by year.
- **Design or defect: a defect.** Duke's design (Oct 1, quoted in `dev/reports/v5-1-private-esp-correction.md`): "A privately owned ESP cuts its prices for customers paying in BU so that it stays revenue neutral. At a 3x conversion rate, a $9 / $12 / $15 menu becomes $3 / $4 / $5 in BU." That price is set at the sale, and so was the step's own first decision ("for BU spent at a private ESP, one BU buys as many essentials as the ESP's conversion rate in dollars"). The code paid the premium a year late, shared by last year's BU, which the design does not have and which makes the cycle. Rule 9: the code did not do what its decision said.
- **Choice (switch `sp.vAt`, a row option of the surplus split; absent or anything but 'sale' = the lagged rule, bit-identical).** Under `vAt: 'sale'` one BU spent at a private ESP buys 1 + vK dollars of essentials, vK = (1 - the workers' match share) x the premium per BU accepted (`bizPremPerBU`: the conversion at `FW.bizRate` under the progressive tax, less face value, less ESP payroll's share, exactly as the year end computes `bizNet` per BU). The BU spent at private ESPs are the share the model already uses to size the PTFs' share (1 - `paW` under open access; all of a non-member's BU otherwise; none of a PTF member's), so each adult's cut is vK x that share x the BU spent, solved with the budget: BU spent = bill / (1 + vK q) when the budget covers it, the whole budget otherwise. The cut is paid as an advance (the private carry goes negative by it) and next year's private premium repays it; the workers' match is paid from that premium at the share in force at the sale. What the premium leaves after the repayment is the premium on ESP payroll BU returned the next year (d73: the payroll pool an ESP cannot pay to its participating workers is converted a year later); that part cannot be known at the sale and is shared as before, by last year's BU. A shortfall carries.
- **Alternatives.** (a) Keep the lag and state the cycle as a limit (the step's default until now); not taken: the lag is not the design. (b) Smooth the pool (two-year average); not taken: a second invented lag. (c) Fix the PTFs' price cut too; not taken: a surplus split distributed after the year is a reading of the PTFs' design (their premium is split three ways once the year's surplus is known), and with the private price at the sale it shows no cycle. (d) Make 'sale' the default now; not taken: every published programme figure since v5.0 uses the private rule, and the OSF-registered v5.9 model must stay reproducible. The default changes only with a preregistered rerun (research-update `prereg/2026-11-s90-private-price-at-sale.md`).
- **Result (tool, seed 1, 500 adults, 20 years).** BU spent per adult, Reference: $16,815, $16,590, $17,392, $17,592, $17,981, then within $16,236-18,195; income $60,376, $79,466, $85,342, $88,216, $92,651 (smooth). Adverse and Stress the same. vK = 0.897 in phase 1 (0.807 in phase 2) in Reference and Adverse, 0.794 (0.715) in Stress. The premium left after the repayment is $305, $73 and $4 per adult in years 1-3 (payroll returned while workers' caps bind), then zero; nothing stays in the carry.
- **Reach (inspection, seeds 1-2, main row, 20 years; not a result).** About 580-600 of the 991 output keys move. The programme's effect on basket poverty: Reference -32.32 to -32.99 points, Adverse -41.05 to -41.73, Stress -40.77 to -41.34; FGT2 about 0.1 points more; median real wealth +$856 (Reference), +$1,179 (Adverse), +$228 (Stress). Every published programme figure since v5.0 (Oct 2) uses the private rule: the v5.9 main rows and readings (`r2-*-104691f`), its tables, erosion and suite folders, the central-bank and history studies, S82, and the v5.0-v5.6 panels.
- **Proofs.** Guard test identical (25 rows x 20 seeds x 483 outputs, three environments). `validate` passed. Five new tests in `privUnitSuite`: the repayment leaves exactly the private share of the returned payroll premium (worst gap 1e-14); each year's private cuts = vK x the BU spent at private ESPs + the lagged share (1.5e-14; with no match and no payroll vK equals the year end's premium per BU); the year-to-year change in BU spent falls from 45.9% to 0.6% (Reference, seed 1, framework run); no accounting identity fails in the main row in three environments (63 premium checks); no random draw added. The conversion tax formula moved unchanged into `bizTaxRates` (one formula for the year end and the sale).

=== The earlier design note that the fix relies on (Oct 2, 2026) ===
# Correction: privately owned essential-service businesses pass the conversion premium to customers

Oct 2, 2026. Design note before code. Written by Claude.

## What changes, in plain words

An essential-service business (an ESP: a grocer, a utility, a clinic, a restaurant) that accepts Basic Units (BU) converts them into dollars at more than face value. The session-30 build gave that extra amount (the "premium") to the owners of privately owned ESPs, shared by wealth. That was wrong. Duke's design, as he described it on Oct 1:

> A privately owned ESP cuts its prices for customers paying in BU so that it stays revenue neutral. At a 3x conversion rate, a $9 / $12 / $15 menu becomes $3 / $4 / $5 in BU.

So the premium becomes **lower prices for the customer**, not profit for the owner. The business takes in the same dollars per meal as before (3 BU converted at 3x is $9). Owners still compete for workers, so **workers at private ESPs earn what a worker at a profit-sharing (community-owned) ESP earns**.

## How the model will do it (Claude's decisions)

1. **Price.** For BU spent at a private ESP, one BU buys as many essentials as the ESP's conversion rate in dollars (at 3x, 1 BU buys $3 of essentials). The ESP's dollar revenue per item is unchanged. No premium goes to owners.
2. **What this does to the money supply.** The Source (the Treasury that issues BU and pays conversions) pays out the full market value of the essentials the customer received, and nothing more. Under the old branch, the owners' premium was new money with no goods behind it. Under the correction, every converted dollar at a private ESP pays for goods actually delivered. That should reduce the price rises that the session-30 restudy found in the Adverse and Stress environments (23-51% a year). I will report what happens, not assume it.
3. **Participants need fewer BU for the same essentials.** BU they do not need expire and go back to the Source, as the session-30 financing already does. The monthly BU amount is not changed.
4. **Capacity still limits it.** A private ESP can only sell as much as it can supply. That limit is built in the creative-output step (d139: an ESP's octave cap follows its capacity), so the two steps are built together and tested together.
5. **Worker pay.** Participating workers at private ESPs receive the same profit-share amount per worker as participating workers at community-owned ESPs (your earlier rule: only participating ESP workers share). The model has no individual firms, so the report will say plainly that this pay is assumed to be funded by the extra sales that lower prices bring.
6. **A check on that assumption (shown, not hidden).** A second row caps the private-ESP pay rise at the profit margin on the added sales, using the published margin for retail, food service and utilities (BEA corporate profits by industry and Census Annual Retail Trade Survey sales; exact tables cited in the code). If the cap binds, the report says how far the design's pay match exceeds what added sales can fund.

## Switches and checks

- New switch `SURP_PRIV`: `'owners'` (the first v5.0 candidate's behaviour) or `'prices'` (the correction, used for v5.0). With `'owners'` every output is bit-identical to the first v5.0 candidate (proved by a full-output diff).
- No new random draws (the eight-draws-per-adult-year guarantee holds).
- Unit tests: (a) an ESP's dollar revenue per unit is the same in both branches; (b) at rate r, 1 BU buys r dollars of essentials at a private ESP; (c) no premium reaches owners under `'prices'`; (d) a participating private-ESP worker gets the same profit share as a community-ESP worker; (e) the margin-capped row never pays more than the margin on added sales.
- Restudy: seeds 1-500, paired, Reference, Adverse and Stress; poverty below the cost of living (basket), wealth poverty, days of basic living covered (BLEI), cost, work, prices, and participants against non-participants.

## What Duke should check

Only this: is "the premium becomes lower prices for BU customers, and private-ESP workers are paid like profit-share workers" what you meant? Everything else is a modelling decision recorded in `dev/DECISIONS.md`.

## Built (Oct 2, 2026), and one change from the plan above

Built as switch `SURP.priv = 'prices'` in `harness.js`, with 6 unit tests (`privUnitSuite`). With the old setting every output is identical to the first v5.0 candidate (full output of `testbed 10 release` in all three environments diffed).

**One change from point 6 above.** I planned to fund the workers' pay match from "the extra sales lower prices bring", with a row capping it at the profit margin on those sales. The model has a fixed basket: lower BU prices let participants buy the same essentials with fewer BU, so there are no extra sales to fund anything. Instead, the match comes out of the premium itself: a private ESP gives its workers the same fraction of its premium that a community ESP gives its workers (one third until there is enough community capacity, then 40%), and the rest becomes lower BU prices. Every worker who takes part then gets the same profit share, wherever they work, and every dollar stays accounted for. A second row gives the whole premium to lower prices (no match), so you can see the difference.

## Results: 500 paired runs, against the first v5.0 candidate (`dev/runs/step14-priv-500-*.txt`)

| | Reference | Adverse | Stress |
|---|---|---|---|
| Below the cost of living, share of adult-years | **30.0% → 22.6%** | **51.7% → 44.5%** | 67.5% → 66.6% |
| Too little wealth at year 20 | **47.5% → 40.4%** | 87.0% → 90.4% (worse) | 89.3% → 91.3% (worse) |
| Real resources a year, adults who did not take part, against no programme | +$3,167 → −$1,071 | +$4,655 → +$1,380 | +$3,059 → +$422 |

In everyday words:

- **At Reference the correction helps on every measure.** Participants' BU go further at private businesses, so fewer people live below the cost of living and fewer end with too little savings.
- **In Adverse and Stress it lowers income poverty but slightly raises wealth poverty**, because the BU freed by lower prices go on to pay project work, which adds new money and prices rise a little faster.
- **Adults who do not take part lose the most.** Under the first v5.0 candidate, they received part of the premium as business owners. Now they receive none of it, and at Reference they end up with slightly less real income than with no programme (−$1,071 a year), because prices still rise. This is what the corrected design implies in the model, and the page says so.
- I expected the correction to slow price rises (point 2 above). It did not: the model already counted the owners' dollars as new money, and the freed BU add a little more. I report this as it came out.

=== The preregistration of the rerun ===
# Preregistration: the private businesses' BU price at the sale (S90's fix), rerun of the v5.9 main rows

Committed Nov 18, 2026 by S90, before any run. Engine: compassionism-simulation at commit `ENGINE_HASH` (main, after pull request PR_NUMBER), which adds the option `sp.vAt: 'sale'` (off by default; with it off every output equals v5.9's, guard test identical).

## Why
S90 traced the damped two-year swing in the BU each adult spends (main row, Reference, seed 1: $22,838 in years 0-1, then $10,969, $21,452, $13,819, $19,472, $16,202) to the private businesses' lower BU price. The code paid it from last year's premium, shared by last year's BU. Duke's design sets it at the sale ("At a 3x conversion rate, a $9 / $12 / $15 menu becomes $3 / $4 / $5 in BU", Oct 1, quoted in compassionism-simulation `dev/reports/v5-1-private-esp-correction.md`). So the lag is a defect (research rule 9), and the swing reaches incomes, BU spent and expired, project hiring and programme cost by year. The fix: under `vAt: 'sale'` a BU spent at a private business buys 1 + vK dollars, where vK is that BU's premium after the conversion tax, payroll and the workers' match. The cut is paid as an advance that next year's premium repays exactly. Only the premium on payroll BU returned a year later (d73) is still shared a year late. Full record: compassionism-simulation `dev/DECISIONS.md` "S90" and `dev/reports/s90-private-price-at-sale.md`. Every published programme figure since v5.0 (Oct 2, 2026) uses the lagged rule. A first look on seeds 1-2 (inspection, not a result) moved the main row's cut in basket poverty by about 0.6-0.7 points.

## Questions
- Q1. Does the at-sale price remove the swing in every environment? Answer: the swing measure below, at the sale against lagged, per environment.
- Q2. How much do the v5.9 headline effects change (the five headline measures, both designs, three environments, 20 and 40 years)? Answer: the paired change, at the sale minus lagged, with its 95% interval.
- Q3. Does any headline statement on the findings page change in sign or in its stated rounding? Answer: a yes/no per statement, read under decision rule 4.

## Design
- **Rows.** The v5.9 main rows as `r2.js --part=M` builds them (no programme; the full-coverage design; the opt-in design), each programme row run twice: lagged (the published setting) and at the sale (`sp: Object.assign({}, row.sp, {vAt: 'sale'})`). The no-programme row does not read the option (it has no surplus split) and is run once.
- **Environments:** Reference, Adverse, Stress. **Horizons:** 20 and 40 years. **Adults:** 500. **Seeds:** 1-500, paired across all rows (common random numbers).
- **Where:** GitHub Actions (`run-study` in compassionism-sim-results; free), a new job `runner/jobs/s90.js` added by pull request before the dispatch. It builds the rows exactly as `r2.js --part=M` does, adds the at-sale copies, and calls the engine's `startRelease({baseline: true})`. Study ids `s90-sale-ENV-YRS`, folders `s90-sale-ENV-YRS-<engine, 7 characters>` with `run.txt` and `SHA256SUMS`.
- **Swing measure (Q1).** Run on the session machine with `node dev/tools/s90_trace.js` (compassionism-simulation; read-only probes, `--check` proves the copy's outputs equal the harness's), seeds 1-20, 500 adults, 20 years, three environments, lagged and `--sale`. It is the mean over years 2-12 of |BU spent per programme adult this year − last year| / this year.

## Checks (before any outcome is read)
1. The lagged programme rows and the no-programme row equal the published `r2-m-ENV-YRS-104691f` rows per seed, on every output key (the option is off on them).
2. Every folder has 500 seeds per row, its engine commit, a clean engine, and `run.txt` and `SHA256SUMS`.
3. The engine's accounting checks (`ACCT`) pass on the at-sale rows for seeds 1-5 in each environment (no identity fails; the premium identity included), run with the unit suite's method.

## Outcomes
- **Primary** (main row against no programme, per design, environment and horizon; as REPRODUCE.md's "Headline values" table defines them): below 30 days of basic living (unweighted); below the cost of living, basket poverty (unweighted); too little wealth, yearly average (unweighted); median real wealth in year-0 dollars (weighted); programme inflation (basket index above no programme, points a year).
- **Secondary:** FGT2 (poverty severity); mean real income; BU spent and BU expired per programme adult (20-year mean); programme cost (the testbed's cost keys); the weighted versions of the primary measures where the published tables give them.
- Gains are confirmed on basket poverty and wealth poverty, not FGT2 alone.

## Analysis
- For each outcome, cell (design × environment × horizon): the effect against no programme under each rule and the paired change (at the sale − lagged), mean over seeds 1-500, with a 95% paired bootstrap interval (2,000 resamples, generator seed 9001).
- The analysis script is added to compassionism-simulation (`dev/tools/s90_tables.py`) before the results are read; it prints checks 1-2 first and stops if one fails.
- No synergy claim is made (one change, not a factorial).
- Multiple comparisons: Holm across the five primary outcomes within each cell, for the statement "the change is not zero"; every interval is published unadjusted as well.

## Decision rules
1. If check 1, 2 or 3 fails, stop: nothing is read, the defect is found, and the run is redone after a dated amendment.
2. Q1: the fix is taken to work if, in every environment, the at-sale swing measure is below half the lagged one. If it is not, stop and report; the default does not change.
3. If rule 2 holds, the at-sale price is the corrected model. Its figures replace the main rows' figures at the next release (Duke assigns the version), with an entry in the Hub's corrections log. The lagged figures stay published as the v5.9 record (the OSF registration is the frozen v5.9 model). This holds whichever way the figures move.
4. Q3: a findings-page statement changes if the at-sale effect changes sign, or if its rounding as printed changes. Each changed statement is listed with both figures.
5. Every other published study that runs programme rows (the main rows' readings, financed rows and 10,000-adult rows, `r2-s/f/b`; the central-bank study `s74-final-3beb5ff`; the history study `s75-eras-e5649ef`; the supply study S82; the suite folders `x2`, `x3`, `x4`; the v5.0-v5.6 panels) gets a dated note on its page or report: it paid the private price a year late, the main row's change was the figure Q2 found, and a rerun is or is not planned. A rerun of any of them is its own preregistered amendment.

## Reporting
Every cell above is published in compassionism-sim-results and in the plain-words report, including changes against the programme and changes too small to matter.

## Amendments
Dated, with the reason, below this line. Nothing above changes after the first run.
